(p-184)Surah 98: Al-Bayyinah

Medinan, though this is disputed, and its verses number eight.

﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book⁠﻿ ... ﴾ That is, the Jews and the Christians. Their being mentioned under this designation serves to indicate the reason for what is attributed to them of the promise to follow the truth, for the basis of that is that they found it in their Book. The relative clause is expressed as a verb because their disbelief occurred after their prophets.

﴿And the polytheists﴾, that is, the worshippers of idols. It has been read as "wal-mushrikūna" (and the polytheists), in coordination with the relative pronoun. ﴿Were not going to abandon﴾, that is, from what they were upon of the promise to follow the truth and to believe in the Messenger who would be sent at the end of time, and the resolve to fulfil it. This promise from the People of the Book is beyond doubt, to the extent that they used to seek victory (yastaftihūna) and say: "O God, grant us victory and help us through the Prophet who will be sent at the end of time." They would also say to their enemies among the polytheists: "The time of a prophet has drawn near who will come confirming what we have said, and we will kill you alongside him with the killing of ʿĀd and Iram." As for the polytheists, it is likely that this occurred among their later generations after this had spread among the People of the Book and they had come to believe its truth, having witnessed their victory over their forebears, as is evidenced by the fact that they used to ask them about the Messenger of God ﷺ: whether he was the one mentioned in their Book, and they used to incite them to alter his attributes, upon him be peace. The "infikāk" (disengagement) of one thing from another means that it separates from it after being joined, like a bone when it dislocates from its joint. This also indicates the completeness of their resolve in the promise, that is: they were not departing from the aforementioned promise; rather, they were united upon it, determined to fulfil it.

﴿Until there comes to them the clear proof (al-bayyinah)﴾, which they had made the arrival of as the appointed time for the unity of word and agreement upon the truth; so they made it the appointed time for separation, division and breaking the promise. The expression of its arrival in the present tense (ya'tīhim) is by consideration of the state of the narrated matter, not by consideration of the state of the narration, as in His exalted saying: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾, that is, what they recited (talat).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a Messenger﴾ is a *badal* (apposition) of "the clear proof" (*al-bayyinah*). He, peace be upon him, was described as the clear proof to signify the utmost clarity of his matter and that he is the promised one mentioned in the two Scriptures. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from God﴾ is connected to an implied verb and is an attribute of "a Messenger," emphasizing, through the added attribution, the grandeur that the *tanwin* (nunation) conveys of his inherent dignity. The meaning is: a Messenger, and what a Messenger, coming from Him, Exalted is He. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿reciting﴾ is another attribute of him, or a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase that precedes it. ﴿purified pages﴾ means free from falsehood, such that falsehood does not approach it from before it or behind it, or that those who are not purified should not touch it. The attribution of their recitation to him, peace be upon him, is because reciting what is in them is equivalent to reciting them themselves. (p-185)

In his commentary on verse 98:3, Abu al-Su'ud says: "His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Therein are books of upright content﴾ is an attribute (sifah) of 'pages' (suhufan), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from their pronoun in 'purified' (mutahharah). It is also permissible that the attribute or the circumstantial clause is only the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa-al-majrur), with 'books' (kutubun) raised by it as the agent (ʿala al-fa'iliyyah). The meaning of 'upright' (qayyimah) is: straight, speaking with truth and correctness."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 98, verse 4:

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Nor did those who were given the Scripture become divided﴾ ...etc., are a statement brought to the purpose of condemning the People of the Book in particular, and of making their crimes more grievous, by clarifying that the separation attributed to them did not arise from any ambiguity in the matter. Rather, it occurred after the truth had become clear, the situation had been made evident, and all excuses had been completely cut off. This is the secret behind describing them as those "given the Scripture," which indicates their complete capacity to study it and to comprehend what it contains of rulings and reports, among which are the descriptions of the Prophet (ﷺ), after their having been mentioned earlier by a designation that functions as a collective noun for both groups. Since these people and the polytheists, by virtue of their agreement on the aforementioned opinion, were regarded as a single group, the separation that proceeded from them after agreement was expressed when reporting its occurrence as "separation." And when explaining how it occurred, it was expressed as "division," in consideration of the independence of each of the two groups of the People of the Book, and as an indication that their departure from the aforementioned opinion was not by way of agreement upon another opinion, but by way of their long-standing disagreement.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿except after the clear proof had come to them﴾, form an istithna' mufarragh (an exception with no stated subject, in which the excepted element is governed by the verb preceding it) taken from the most general category of times. That is: they did not divide at any time except after the clear evidence had come to them, the evidence that plainly indicates that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the one promised in their Scripture, an indication that is evident and beyond doubt. This is like His words, the Exalted: ﴿Nor did those who were given the Scripture differ except after knowledge had come to them﴾.

The author's statement, "And they were not commanded except to worship God" (﴿وَما أُمِرُوا إلا لِيَعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾), is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah) that serves to emphasize how ugly their conduct was. The meaning is: while the situation was that they had been commanded in their Book only to worship God. It has also been said that the lām here carries the sense of "an" (that), meaning: "except that they worship God." This is reinforced by the recitation (qirā'ah) "illā an yaʿbudū Allāh."

﴿مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ﴾ means making their religion sincerely (khāliṣan) for Him, Exalted is He; or making themselves sincerely devoted to Him, Exalted is He, in religion.

﴿حُنَفاءَ﴾ means inclining away from all deviant beliefs toward Islam. ﴿وَيُقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ ويُؤْتُوا الزَّكاةَ﴾: if by these two is meant the prayer and almsgiving in their own law (sharīʿah), then the matter is clear. If what is meant is the prayer and almsgiving in our law, then the meaning of commanding them with these in the two Books is that commanding them to follow our law is a command to them to observe all its rulings, of which these two are a part.

﴿وَذَلِكَ﴾ refers to what has been mentioned: worshipping God, sincerity, establishing the prayer, and giving the zakat. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is to indicate the loftiness of its rank and the exaltedness of its station. ﴿دِينُ القَيِّمَةِ﴾ means the religion of the upright community (al-millah al-qayyimah). It has been read as "ad-dīn al-qayyimah," interpreting religion (dīn) as community (millah).

Here it has been said: God's statement, ﴿لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ up to His statement ﴿كُتُبٌ قَيِّمَةٌ﴾ [Q 98:1–3], is a report of what they used to say before his (ﷺ) mission, namely that they would not part from their religion until his mission, and they promised that they would part from it at that time and unite upon the truth.

God's statement ﴿وَما تَفَرَّقَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ﴾ [Q 98:4] and so on, is an explanation of their breaking their promise and their reversing the matter, by making what was the cause of their separation from their false religion, as they had promised, into a cause of their steadfastness in it and their not parting from it.

A similar case is a poor sinner who says to one who admonishes him: "I will not part from what I am in until I become wealthy." He becomes wealthy and increases in sin, so his admonisher says to him: "You were not parted from sin until you became rich, and you only clung to sin after you became affluent?"

You know well that this only holds after the previous discussion, on the assumption that by "separation" (tafarruq) is meant their separation from the truth, such that it is said: separation from the truth entails steadfastness in falsehood, so it is as if it were said: "They did not unite upon their religion except after the clear proof had come to them." As for the assumption that by it is meant their dispersing into sects, such that some of them believed, some denied, and some knew and yet were obstinate, as the questioner permitted, then no. So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 98, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell.﴾ This is an explanation of the state of the two groups in the Hereafter, after an explanation of their state in this world. He mentioned the polytheists so that it would not be supposed that the ruling is specific to the People of the Book, in accordance with the specificity of witnessing the signs of prophethood in the Scripture to them. The meaning of their being "in it" is that they will arrive at it on the Day of Resurrection. The use of the nominal sentence serves to indicate that its content will certainly be realized. Or it may mean that they are in it now, either by treating their being engaged in what necessitates it as being equivalent to their being engaged in it itself, or on the basis that what they are in of disbelief and sins is the very substance of the Fire, except that it has appeared in this life in accidental forms, and they will strip it off in the next life and it will appear in its true form, as was mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾ in Surat al-A'raf.

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in the predicate. The sharing of the two groups in entering the abode of punishment by way of eternal abiding does not contradict the difference of their punishment in its manner, for Hell has degrees (darakat), and its punishments are of various kinds. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to them in consideration of their being characterized by the vile qualities mentioned, and the sense of distance contained in it is for the sake of indicating the extreme remoteness of their rank in evil; that is, those far-removed ones mentioned. ﴿They are the worst of creation﴾: the worst of the created beings, that is, in deeds. This agrees with what will come concerning the believers, so it falls within the scope of a causal explanation for their eternal abiding in the Fire; or their worst in station and destination, so it serves as an emphasis on the grievousness of their condition. It has also been read with a hamza, according to the original form.

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ explains the good conditions of the believers, following the explanation of the wretched state of the disbelievers. This follows the Qur'anic pattern (sunnah, here meaning the established method) of pairing warning (tarhib) with encouragement (targhib).

﴿Those﴾, who are described with what is at the furthest reach of nobility and excellence, namely faith and obedience, ﴿are the best of creation﴾. It has also been read (qira'ah, a canonical mode of recitation) as "خِيارُ البَرِيَّةِ" (khiyar al-bariyyah). This is the plural of "خَيِّرٍ" (khayyir), like "جَيِّدٍ" (jayyid) and "جِيادٍ" (jiyad).

(p-187)﴿Their reward﴾ in return for the faith and obedience they had, ﴿with their Lord is Gardens of Eden beneath which rivers flow﴾. If by "gardens" is meant trees with intertwined branches, as is the apparent sense, then the flowing of the rivers beneath them is evident. If by "gardens" is meant the whole ground and what is upon it, then it is according to the visible part. In either case, what is meant is that the rivers flow without a trench (ukhdud).

﴿Abiding therein forever﴾, enjoying the various kinds of physical and spiritual blessings. In mentioning their praise first with being the best (of creation), and in mentioning the reward, which indicates that what they are given is in return for what they were described with, and in showing that it comes from Him, the Exalted, and in the reference to the title of Lordship (rububiyyah, the lordship that signifies nurturing and bringing to perfection) together with its attribution to their pronoun, and in the plural of "gardens" and its restriction by the genitive construction, and by what increases its bliss, and in the emphasis of eternity with abadan (forever), there is an indication of the utmost goodness of their condition, which is not hidden.

﴿God is well pleased with them﴾: this is a resumptive clause explaining what He bestows upon them additionally, beyond the mentioned recompense for their deeds.

﴿And they are well pleased with Him﴾, in that they have attained the furthest of their demands and possessed the summit of their aims, and there has been made available to them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

﴿That﴾, namely what has been mentioned of reward and good pleasure, ﴿is for him who fears his Lord﴾. Indeed, fear, which is among the distinguishing traits of the scholars concerning the affairs of God, the Mighty and Majestic, is the basis for all the perfections, both theoretical and practical, that lead to religious and worldly happiness. The reference to the title of Lordship (rububiyyah), which expresses ownership and nurturing, is to indicate the cause of the fear, and a warning against being deceived by (His) nurturing.

On the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Bayyinah, ["Lam yakun"], will be on the Day of Resurrection with the best of creation, in the evening and in the resting place."
